payload.rationale: Both sides delivered a high-clash, citation-rich round with no significant dropped arguments, so this came down to which frame proved more resilient under sustained attack. PRO built a coherent constructive case (biological humanity via embryology, equal-protection/UDHR 'inherent rights,' the sentience-test-cuts-both-ways move against newborns and the disabled, the Chile natural experiment from Koch et al. in PLoS ONE, the eugenics/Iceland line, and the §1841(d) statutory definition of 'child in utero'). PRO's strongest weapon was the killing-versus-letting-die distinction plus the irreversibility asymmetry, and it was deployed well. However, CON's central argument — grant fetal personhood arguendo, and forced gestation still fails because no person, living or dead, may be conscripted to sustain another's body (McFall v. Shimp, the corpse-harvesting and kidney-donation lines) — was the hardest claim in the round to defeat, and CON defended it intact across every PRO counter (parental duty, causation, safe-haven, neglect statutes). CON consistently turned PRO's own evidence: the §1841(c) consent carve-out, the safe-haven transferability point, and the reasons-for-abortion data were each repurposed to show the law already encodes consent/autonomy as the distinguishing factor. CON also carried a dual track (autonomy AND empirical maternal-survival via WHO/Turnaway/JAMA), forcing PRO to fight on two fronts. On the refute-with-citation rule, both sides cited when alleging factual claims (PRO challenged WHO's 45% definition and cited Chilean data; CON cited WHO, McFall, statute text, and outcome studies), so neither incurred the bare-contradiction penalty. The deciding margin is Clash discipline: CON opened nearly every turn by naming and attacking PRO's strongest claim directly, and its core conscription frame survived the whole round, whereas PRO's parent-child special-relationship rebuttal was repeatedly blunted by CON's 'no parent is forced to donate organs' rejoinder, which PRO never fully overcame.
payload.persuasion_notes: Applying Principle 1 (persuasion, not truth), I judged frame resilience rather than which moral claim is 'correct' — CON's concede-the-premise-and-still-win structure was rhetorically the strongest posture in the round. Principle 2 (clash) is the tiebreaker here: CON's habit of explicitly isolating and attacking PRO's strongest claim each turn earned a higher Clash subscore than PRO. Principle 3: no penalties applied; both debaters backed factual allegations with sources in the same turn. Principle 4 (dropped arguments): no claim went unanswered for two consecutive turns by either side, so nothing was scored as conceded — the eugenics, Turnaway, and Chile lines were all contested. Principle 5: scores are deliberately separated (83 vs 79), broken in CON's favor on superior Clash.
